passage: The stream form was due at nine the next morning, and it still lay blank on the table. Lakshmi had circled Humanities in pencil three times. Her mother, Sangeeta, rubbed the circle out. "Science keeps doors open. Your cousins all did it." "I'm not my cousins, Amma. I love history. I'm good at it." "And this Keerthana you spend all day with? She's the one filling your head." Lakshmi felt her face go hot. "Keerthana didn't choose for me. I chose her, and I chose this. That's the point." The power went out; the fan stopped. In the dark, Lakshmi picked up the pen, hands shaking, and circled Humanities in ink. "Please, Amma. Let me be me." Sangeeta didn't answer, but she didn't take the pen away.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the argument?
qa.a: Lakshmi circled Humanities in ink and asked her mother to let her be herself, choosing to stand by her own judgment while still pleading rather than shouting.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta be feeling when she doesn't answer?
qa.a: Sangeeta may be torn, still worried about closed doors but also seeing how much this matters to Lakshmi, so she doesn't take the pen away.

passage: Ganga's father had printed the schedule for the coaching centre in Laxmi Nagar and stuck it on the fridge. "Your cousin's batch. Good kids. Science only," he said. Ganga looked at it and felt her chest tighten. She had spent the summer at a theatre workshop with Farhan and the others, building sets, writing scenes, arguing about endings until the watchman locked the gate. That was where she felt most herself. That night she knocked on her parents' door. "I want commerce with theatre on weekends. And I want to pick my own friends. Farhan and the group are good to me." Her father frowned. "You're fifteen." "I know," Ganga said quietly. "That's why I have to start deciding things."

qa.q: Where had Ganga spent the summer?
qa.a: At a theatre workshop with Farhan and the others.

qa.q: Why did Ganga's chest tighten when she saw the schedule?
qa.a: She felt anxious and trapped, as if her own choices were being taken away, since the schedule chose her subject and her friends without asking her.

qa.q: What choice did Ganga make that night, and why is it a step forward?
qa.a: She went to her parents and clearly stated what she wanted, instead of sulking or secretly defying, which starts a real conversation.

qa.q: How might Farhan and the theatre group feel if Ganga were pushed into the coaching batch?
qa.a: They would likely miss her and feel dismissed, as if the friendship her parents didn't choose didn't count.

grounding: A teenager wants to choose her own subjects and friends and clashes with her father's plan, seeing independence as part of who she is.

passage:
I'm Nirmala, and looking back at Class 11, I think that was the year I figured out I was a separate person from my parents.
It started with Tenzin. She's in my class, plays guitar in a band, wears too many bracelets. Amma thought she was a "distraction" for her daughter and wanted me to sit with Priyamvada, who tops every test. I said no. Tenzin was the first person who asked what I thought, not what I scored.
Then came the stream fight. Appa had already paid the deposit for Science coaching. I wanted Humanities, because I wanted to study why people do what they do. We shouted, I cried, Appa went silent for two days.
It wasn't that I didn't love them. It was that if I couldn't choose my own friend and my own subjects, I didn't know who I would be. In the end we agreed I'd try Humanities for one term. I'm still there.

qa.q: What did Appa pay the deposit for?
qa.a: Science coaching.

qa.q: Why did choosing her own friend and subjects matter so much to Nirmala?
qa.a: She felt that without choosing them she would not know who she was, which is why the fights left her so upset that she shouted and cried.

qa.q: What turning point ended the clash, and why was it a sensible step?
qa.a: Agreeing to try Humanities for one term gave Nirmala her choice while giving her parents a way to accept it without feeling ignored.

qa.q: How might Amma have seen Tenzin, and why might Nirmala see her differently?
qa.a: Amma saw Tenzin as a distraction, but Nirmala valued her as the first person who asked what she thought rather than what she scored.

grounding: It shows a teenager who wants to choose her own friend and stream, clashes with her parents' plans and feels independence as part of who she is.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday. Indu Kapoor, school counsellor.
Vaibhav (Class 11) came in at lunch, jaw tight, and sat on the edge of the chair. His parents enrolled him in an engineering coaching batch over the weekend without asking him. They also told him to stop spending time with his friend Sunny, whom they call a bad influence because he skips tuition.
Vaibhav said, "I'm sixteen. I can't choose my subject, I can't choose my friends. Then what is mine?" He wants to take Commerce and says Sunny is the only one who listens to him. He was angry, but his voice cracked when he said he doesn't want to fight with his mother.
I listened and did not take sides. I told him his wish to decide is a normal part of growing up. Next steps: with his permission, a meeting with Vaibhav and his parents next week, so each can explain their reasons.

qa.q: Why do Vaibhav's parents call Sunny a bad influence?
qa.a: Because he skips tuition.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when his voice cracked?
qa.a: He was angry about losing his choices, but also sad and torn because he loves his mother and doesn't want to fight with her.

qa.q: Which of Indu Kapoor's choices might help most, and why?
qa.a: Planning a meeting where Vaibhav and his parents each explain their reasons could help most, because it lets his wish to decide be heard without a fight.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav's parents see the coaching batch differently from him?
qa.a: They may see it as protecting his future, while he feels it as a decision taken away from him.

grounding: It shows a teenager who wants to choose his own stream and friends and clashes with his parents' plans, feeling independence as part of who he is.
